source_acquisition.search_note: The PDF homepage/project link and the author project page identify rainarit/metamergen; gh README metadata has the exact paper title, author list, and OpenReview citation. The local corpus/visual_sources/iclr-2026-d2112f671397/ directory is absent. The inventory row says no_public_source_found and automatically suggests ultralytics/ultralytics, but that repository is only cited for YOLOv8 and has no title/project relation, so it is rejected as a visual source. The author-linked repository tree contains rendered website PNGs matching Figures 1, 4, 5, 6, and 13, plus a crop helper, but no matching plot/figure/table generator, paper .tex, notebook, data file, TikZ/PGF source, or style file for Figures 1–16; generic website SVG/icon assets are unrelated. Figures 2, 3, 7–12, and 14–16 therefore remain PDF-rendered evidence rather than editable source-backed objects.

paper_style.palette_strategy: The PDF uses a small semantic palette: exact vector accent #097969 for section/author-linked green text, salmon/pink for own-human-fixation curves, turquoise/green for random or combined streams, orange for peripheral-only, periwinkle/blue for foveal-only or CLIP/DINOv2 contrasts, and light gray grids. Qualitative blocks add red fixation dots and green/red SAME/DIFFERENT borders. Hue is usually paired with marker or line style for quantitative conditions, but several image montages and ablation bars remain largely color-dependent.
paper_style.vector_raster_mix: The body, captions, axes text, and some labels are embedded PDF text/vector objects; most numbered visual composites are raster images embedded in the PDF. Figure 1, Figure 4, and Figure 6 combine raster/diagram content with vector captions, while Figures 2–5 and 7–16 are predominantly raster composites at the PDF object level. The author repository supplies matching rendered PNGs for Figures 1, 4, 5, 6, and 13 but no editable plotting source.
paper_style.style_consistency: Caption typography and the green accent are stable across main and appendix pages, and the own/random condition palette recurs in Figures 4, 5, 7, and 8. Layout grammar is less uniform: quantitative panels vary in label size and legend treatment, while qualitative figures consistently use bordered SAME/DIFFERENT blocks. Raster chart labels are small relative to the embedded Nimbus Roman caption text, and there is no table style because the PDF contains no Table object.

figures.label: Figure 1

caption.text: Figure 1: MetamerGen model architecture. High-resolution and blurred, low-resolution images are processed through DINOv2-Base to extract patch tokens. Foveal features are obtained by applying binary masks to high-resolution patch tokens, retaining only fixated regions. Both foveal and peripheral patch tokens are processed through separate Perceiver-based query networks that compress features into conditioning tokens compatible with Stable Diffusion’s cross-attention mechanism. The resulting dual conditioning streams are integrated into the pretrained UNet.

color.semantic_mapping: Teal/green accents mark the paper and peripheral stream; pastel blocks distinguish foveal/peripheral tokens and the Stable-Diffusion conditioning path; black and gray encode structure and arrows; red marks fixation points.

encodings.line: arrows encode feature flow and cross-attention

figures.data_and_statistics: A mechanism diagram, not a sample-level estimate. It shows two 448×448 inputs, DINOv2-Base patch-token extraction, a fixation mask retaining sparse foveal tokens, an unmasked blurred peripheral stream, separate Perceiver query nets, and dual conditioning into a pretrained Stable Diffusion UNet. The paper specifies 14×14 DINOv2 patches, 1024 input tokens and 32 compressed conditioning tokens in §3.1–3.2; the drawing does not encode training repetitions or uncertainty.
figures.evidence_relation: Introduction scene-understanding claim → §3 foveal/peripheral representation and Eqs. (1)–(5) → this architecture interface → Figures 2–5 quality/feature analyses → Appendix A.3 resampler detail. It explains what is manipulated in later behavioral and ablation comparisons but does not by itself establish the metamer judgment effect.
design_strengths: The shared input-to-UNet flow makes the two conditioning streams and their asymmetry legible at a glance.
The fixation mask, query-net branches, token counts, and cross-attention endpoint provide redundant structural cues.
The page-width placement immediately after the method transition gives the headline mechanism a stable visual anchor.
design_weaknesses: Small embedded labels and pastel token colors are difficult to parse at normal two-column reading size.
The diagram omits adapter parameterization, dropout, guidance weights, and the training-only versus inference-time distinction.
Color carries branch identity more strongly than shape, so the foveal/peripheral contrast weakens in grayscale.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use a matched left/right input pair and a single downstream endpoint, with branch-specific masks and compression blocks, to turn a multimodal conditioning mechanism into an auditable path diagram.

figures.label: Figure 2

caption.text: Figure 2: FID values for different input parameters of MetamerGen. Lower FID indicates closer alignment with real images and better quality.

color.semantic_mapping: Green circles vary peripheral blur/scale with blur fixed at 0.25×; salmon/red squares vary blur; blue dashed line is the SD-1.5 reference. Gray is the plotting grid.

encodings.line: solid trend lines and blue dashed reference
encodings.text: colored markers are explained in adjacent text

figures.data_and_statistics: A single inset plot compares FID10K across a linear peripheral-scale/blur sweep. The green series holds the blur level at 0.25× while changing peripheral scale; the red series changes blur; the blue horizontal dashed line is the Stable Diffusion 1.5 baseline. Lower FID is better. The raster plot gives point trajectories but no seed, sample count, interval, or error encoding.
figures.evidence_relation: §3.4 image-generation-quality setup → this parameter sanity check → behavioral choice of 0.25× blur → Figures 11 and 15 reproduce quality sensitivity under broader blur/token and encoder ablations. It supports the selected operating point, not the causal claim that human fixations improve judgments.
design_strengths: The reference line creates an immediate quality threshold for the two sweeps.
The inset is compact and keeps the parameter decision adjacent to the method/results text.
Linear axes and light two-direction grid support approximate reading of the trend.
design_weaknesses: No formal legend appears inside the plot; series colors are decoded by nearby prose rather than a self-contained key.
FID10K has no uncertainty, denominator, or generation-seed disclosure.
Red/green/blue are not robust to grayscale and are not paired with distinct line/marker semantics for every condition.
figures.reusable_pattern: For a parameter-selection plot, place a clearly labeled baseline beside the sweep and state the direction of the quality metric in the caption; retain an explicit legend when the plot is reused independently.

figures.label: Figure 3

caption.text: Figure 3: Metameric vs. non-metameric judgments. (Left) Original images with human fixations overlaid in red paired with generated images judged as the “same” by participants. (Right) Original images with fixations and generated images judged as “different” by participants. More examples, including generations from random fixations, can be found in Appendix A.6.

color.semantic_mapping: Green border/heading marks participant SAME judgments; red border/heading marks DIFFERENT judgments; red dots mark human fixations; black labels and white image cells provide structural contrast.

figures.data_and_statistics: A dense qualitative grid pairs original scenes with MetamerGen generations. The left green-bordered block contains examples judged “same” under human fixation input; the right red-bordered block contains “different” examples. Red fixation dots are overlaid on originals. There are no numeric axes, aggregation, sample denominator, or uncertainty marks; each image pair is a representative qualitative unit.
figures.evidence_relation: The visual claim in §4.2 and the qualitative lead-in to §5 is: own fixations can produce plausible hypotheses of a viewer’s scene representation. The grid links the real-time task in Figure 6 and the own-fixation behavioral rates to quantitative feature analyses in Figures 4–5; Appendix A.6 extends the same layout in Figures 9–10.
design_strengths: The same layout across outcome classes makes the judgment contrast immediately scannable.
Fixation dots preserve the experimental manipulation instead of showing only polished generations.
Large page-width placement gives enough image area for semantic scene comparison.
design_weaknesses: Representative examples cannot convey the 29.4%/27.7% rates or selection process.
The red fixation overlay can be visually mistaken for a saliency heatmap, and image content is not matched by explicit IDs.
The red/green border semantics are color-dependent despite textual SAME/DIFF labels.
figures.reusable_pattern: Pair representative stimulus and reconstruction cells under explicit outcome headers, and preserve the manipulated fixation overlay so a qualitative montage remains tied to the behavioral protocol.

evidence.label: p.7 Figure 3 qualitative judgment grid and caption

figures.label: Figure 4

caption.text: Figure 4: Multi-level feature analysis pipeline using neurally-grounded model: (Top) Early, mid, and late network layers serve as proxies for different stages of processing across the hierarchy of visual brain areas. (Bottom) Results show that as feature similarity increased at these different processing levels, the proportion of participants judging generated images as metameric also increased. These effects were clearer when metamers were generated based on a viewer’s own fixated locations (salmon) than on randomly-sampled locations (turquoise).

color.semantic_mapping: Salmon circles/solid lines encode own-fixation generations; turquoise/teal squares/dashed lines encode random-fixation generations; gray grid and black annotations are neutral. Exact PDF vector text uses the embedded green accent #097969; curve colors are rendered estimates.

encodings.text: r and p annotations plus stage labels

figures.data_and_statistics: The top pipeline maps original/generated image pairs to early, mid, and late layers of a blur-robust AlexNet aligned to visual brain areas. The bottom has three scatter/line panels with linear feature-similarity x axes and proportion-“same” y axes, salmon own-fixation and turquoise random-fixation series, vertical error bars, and r,p annotations. The plotted uncertainty is visible as error bars, but the caption does not define whether they are SE, SD, or a participant-level interval.
figures.evidence_relation: §5.1 neurally-grounded feature claim → top hierarchy proxy diagram and bottom layer-wise association → supports the mechanism that feature similarity tracks metamer judgments → Figure 5 interpretable features and Appendix Figure 14 stream-specific replication. It is correlational and does not identify a layer as causally sufficient.
design_strengths: The mechanism schematic and aligned three-panel result establish a direct visual bridge from model layer to behavioral outcome.
Own/random condition uses both color and marker/line style, giving better redundancy than color alone.
r,p labels and vertical uncertainty marks expose association strength and variability without a separate legend box.
design_weaknesses: The pipeline and three plots make the page dense; small labels and error bars are hard to read in the two-column PDF.
Uncertainty definition, sample unit, and denominator are absent.
The semantic “higher similarity” direction differs across metrics elsewhere, but this figure uses one generic similarity framing.
figures.reusable_pattern: Place a compact representation hierarchy above aligned per-level association panels, and encode experimental conditions redundantly with hue, marker, and line style while stating the estimand in the caption.

evidence.label: p.8 Figure 4 pipeline, three result panels, and caption

figures.label: Figure 5

caption.text: Figure 5: (Left) Mid-level visual features driving metamer judgments: For metamers generated from the viewer’s own fixation locations (salmon), changes in monocular depth estimates of scene structure strongly predicted “same” judgments to generations. The alignment in proto-object segmentation between original and generated scenes, quantified by mIoU, similarly predicted metamerism rate (higher mIoU scores correlating with higher proportions of “same” judgments), although here the relationship was less pronounced. (Right) High-level visual features driving metamer judgments: Semantic similarity strongly predicts metameric scene understanding, with larger DreamSim distances corresponding to reduced perceptual alignment. CLIP similarity shows a similar trend, but not when scenes were generated from randomly-sampled locations (turquoise).

color.semantic_mapping: Salmon circles/solid lines represent human-fixation generations; turquoise squares/dashed lines represent random-fixation generations; gray grid and black r,p labels are neutral. Green section headings are the PDF accent.

encodings.x: feature score (SiLog, mIoU, CLIP cosine, or DreamSim distance)

figures.data_and_statistics: Four linear scatter/line panels are grouped into two green-headed sections: mid-level depth (SiLog) and proto-object segmentation (mIoU), then high-level CLIP cosine similarity and DreamSim distance. Salmon own-fixation circles/solid lines and turquoise random-fixation squares/dashed lines carry vertical error bars. Direction is metric-specific: lower SiLog/DreamSim distance and higher mIoU/CLIP similarity correspond to more “same” judgments; each panel annotates r,p.
figures.evidence_relation: §5.2 feature-analysis question → stepwise selection of interpretable low/mid/high feature axes → Figure 5 provides mid/high evidence → Appendix A.5 Figures 7–8 adds low-level Gabor and object metrics, while Figure 14 repeats the analysis under stream ablations. It connects semantic/depth mechanisms to the headline judgment outcome but remains associative.
design_strengths: The two section headers establish a useful processing-level hierarchy without adding separate subfigures.
Metric-specific panel titles and r,p annotations keep four heterogeneous measures in one comparison surface.
Condition is redundantly encoded by color, marker, and line style.
design_weaknesses: The caption explains metric directions unevenly and does not define the vertical error bars or the regression/aggregation unit.
Four panels have different feature ranges, so visual slope magnitudes are not directly comparable.
Color contrast and small raster labels reduce accessibility in grayscale or low-resolution reproduction.
figures.reusable_pattern: Group heterogeneous feature probes by processing level, retain a common behavioral y estimand, and state each metric’s direction so readers do not treat all slopes as interchangeable.

evidence.label: p.9 Figure 5 four-panel feature analysis and caption

figures.label: Figure 6

caption.text: Figure 6: Real-time paradigm for determining scene metamers. Each trial begins with drift correction and central fixation, followed by free viewing of an original scene for a predetermined number of fixations. After image offset, participants maintain central fixation for 5 seconds while fixation coordinates are transmitted via API to MetamerGen for real-time image generation. The generated image (or original, depending on the condition) is then presented to the viewer for 200ms, followed by an enforced same-different behavioral judgment via a gamepad within a 10-second response window.

color.semantic_mapping: Green labels and MetamerGen block identify the generation API; black arrows and icons encode temporal order; gray/white boxes are neutral; pink/red accents identify fixation or same/different controls.

figures.data_and_statistics: A left-to-right trial timeline has six stages: drift correction, central fixation, free viewing of the original for 1–10 fixations, a 5 s central fixation/API generation delay, 200 ms generated-or-original presentation, and a 10 s same/different gamepad response. The black execution arrow and stage boxes encode order and timing; there is no axis, sample statistic, or uncertainty.
figures.evidence_relation: Appendix A.1 operationalizes the behavioral task summarized in §4.2 and Figure 3. It supplies the timing and API boundary needed to interpret the own-fixation/random-fixation comparison and the 45-participant/300-trial sampling design; it does not quantify performance itself.
design_strengths: The timeline makes the unusual real-time generation delay and enforced response window explicit.
Timing labels and stage names are redundant with icons and arrow order.
It is an effective appendix interface for reproducing the behavioral protocol.
design_weaknesses: The image is raster and small timing text requires zooming.
Condition randomization, trial counts, and counterbalancing are not represented in the timeline.
The generated-or-original branch is mentioned in the caption but not visually separated into parallel paths.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use a single chronological arrow with numbered/timed stimulus states and an explicit system handoff marker whenever an experiment depends on an online model call.

evidence.label: p.16 Figure 6 behavioral timeline and caption

figures.label: Figure 7

caption.text: Figure 7: Stronger Gabor texture responses than originals coincided with greater proportions of metameric judgments. This suggests that enhanced texture definition, like enhanced edge information, contributes to the perceived realism of generated metamers across multiple spatial frequencies and orientations.

color.semantic_mapping: Salmon/teal curves compare own and random fixation conditions; green bordered qualitative examples encode high/low Gabor response; gray grid and black annotations are neutral.

encodings.x: Gabor response difference for 0°, 45°, and 135° filters
encodings.facet: orientation panels plus high/low response examples

figures.data_and_statistics: The appendix composite contains three small association panels for Gabor orientation differences (0°, 45°, 135°) and a qualitative image comparison indicating increased response-magnitude differences. Axes are linear, curves use own/random conditions with markers, line styles, and vertical error bars, and each plot includes r,p text. The 90° orientation is discussed as non-significant in the surrounding text but is not shown as a panel.
figures.evidence_relation: Appendix A.5.1 extends the low-level feature analysis omitted from main Figure 5. It tests whether stronger generated texture responses predict “same” judgments, links to the Sobel edge-density discussion, and constrains the claim that enhanced texture/edge definition contributes to perceived realism. It is a mechanism correlation, not a causal texture intervention.
design_strengths: The qualitative high/low response examples give visual meaning to otherwise abstract Gabor differences.
Orientation-specific panels make the significant/non-significant coverage explicit in the surrounding text.
Marker and line style redundantly distinguish fixation conditions.
design_weaknesses: The orientation labels and r,p values are tiny, and the omitted 90° result is easy to miss without the prose.
Error bars have no definition or denominator.
The qualitative examples and quantitative panels share a canvas but have no explicit visual separator tying a specific image to a specific orientation.
figures.reusable_pattern: Combine orientation-specific association plots with a small paired stimulus example to connect a low-level filter statistic to the image property that a reader should inspect.

evidence.label: p.18 Figure 7 Gabor panels and qualitative examples

figures.label: Figure 8

caption.text: Figure 8: Object detection errors predict metameric perception: (Top) mAP scores demonstrate that higher precision accuracies (from mAP 60% to mAP 80%) with better alignment at strict localization boundaries correlate with increased “same” metameric judgments. (Bottom) Object detection metrics show a positive relationship where improvements in model precision, recall, and F1 scores correspond to increased “same” metameric judgments.

color.semantic_mapping: Salmon/teal series encode own/random fixation conditions; gray grids and black annotations are neutral; green heading/border identifies the object-localization analysis.

encodings.facet: mAP threshold row versus detection-metric row

figures.data_and_statistics: Six linear association panels are arranged as a 2×3 grid: top row mAP at 60%, 70%, and 80% IoU thresholds; bottom row precision, recall, and F1. Each panel compares salmon own-fixation and teal random-fixation series with circles/squares, solid/dashed lines, vertical error bars, and r,p annotations. The panel titles identify the metric and threshold; no separate legend is drawn.
figures.evidence_relation: Appendix A.5.2 connects YOLOv8 object inventories, class predictions, and localization errors to metamer judgments. It expands the main high/mid-level feature story with object-level precision/recall/localization evidence, and the text interprets a widening own/random gap at stricter mAP thresholds. No object count, confidence threshold, or uncertainty definition is encoded in the figure.
design_strengths: The mAP threshold row distinguishes recognition quality from strict localization, matching the paper’s mechanism claim.
A regular six-panel layout supports metric-by-metric scanning.
Markers, lines, and condition colors provide redundant series identification.
design_weaknesses: Six panels plus annotations are dense at page scale; the plot lacks a legend and relies on surrounding prose for color meaning.
Error bars and r,p annotations are not defined statistically.
The phrase “higher precision accuracies” in the caption can conflate mAP with precision; panel labels must carry the distinction.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use a threshold row above complementary precision/recall/F1 panels when the claim concerns both object recognition and localization, while retaining a common behavioral y axis.

figures.label: Figure 9

caption.text: Figure 9: Additional metameric vs. non-metameric judgment example images based on human fixations. (Left) Original images with human fixations overlaid in red and corresponding generated images judged as “same” by participants. (Right) Original images with fixations and generated images judged as “different” by participants.

color.semantic_mapping: Green and red blocks encode SAME and DIFFERENT judgments; red dots encode human fixation locations; black labels and neutral image backgrounds carry the layout.

encodings.text: ORIGINAL, SAME, DIFF and fixation-dot labels

figures.data_and_statistics: A dense two-block montage repeats the Figure 3 grammar with additional human-fixation examples: original images with red fixation dots and generated images judged same on the left, and different on the right. It has no quantitative axes, legend, metric, denominator, or uncertainty encoding.
figures.evidence_relation: Appendix A.6 is the qualitative extension explicitly promised by Figure 3’s caption. The object supports reproducibility of the visual judgment categories and shows variation beyond the main examples, but it cannot estimate the own-fixation same rate or explain participant-level disagreement.
design_strengths: The repeated layout makes Figure 9 directly comparable to Figure 3.
Fixation overlays preserve the input condition rather than presenting unconditioned image pairs.
The page-width canvas accommodates enough examples to show scene diversity.
design_weaknesses: The selection rule for “additional” examples is not stated.
Dense small image cells make object identity and fixation locations hard to inspect without zoom.
Outcome colors are not grayscale-safe even though text headers partially recover the distinction.
figures.reusable_pattern: Reuse the main qualitative grid as an appendix replication surface, but label the input condition in the figure title and state how examples were selected.

figures.label: Figure 10

caption.text: Figure 10: Additional metameric vs. non-metameric judgment example images based on randomly-sampled fixations. (Left) Original images with randomly-sampled fixations overlaid in red and corresponding generated images judged as “same” by participants. (Right) Original images with fixations and generated images judged as “different” by participants.

color.semantic_mapping: Green/red outcome blocks encode SAME/DIFFERENT; red dots identify sampled fixation coordinates; black labels and neutral cells define image roles.

figures.data_and_statistics: The montage repeats Figure 9’s two-column qualitative grammar for randomly sampled fixations. Red dots show random fixation coordinates on originals; the left block contains same judgments and the right block different judgments. No axes, legend, aggregation, uncertainty, or image-level IDs are provided.
figures.evidence_relation: Appendix A.6 complements Figure 9 and isolates the random-fixation input condition used in the main behavioral comparison. It helps assess qualitative plausibility under random sampling but does not replace the 27.7% random-condition estimate or its statistical comparison.
design_strengths: Keeping the layout identical to Figure 9 makes the fixation-source contrast easy to compare.
The red dots expose the sampling manipulation directly on each source image.
The outcome headers are understandable without a metric legend.
design_weaknesses: Random and human fixation examples are not paired to the same underlying scenes, so visual differences may reflect sample composition.
No selection or balancing rule is given for the examples.
Small cells and red overlays are difficult to read in grayscale and at normal PDF zoom.
figures.reusable_pattern: Hold the qualitative layout constant across sampling conditions and change only the visible fixation source, so readers can inspect the manipulation without learning a new visual grammar.

figures.label: Figure 11

caption.text: Figure 11: Influence of blur-level and foveal token count on image generation quality. (Top Row) Image generation quality decreases as greater blur degrades the base image. (Bottom Row) Image generation quality increases as a function of increasing foveal tokens.

color.semantic_mapping: The top row uses panel titles to distinguish CLIP cosine, DreamSim distance, and FID10K; the bottom row changes foveal-token count. Salmon/teal/blue metric strokes are rendered estimates; gray grid is neutral.

encodings.x: ordered blur levels 28×28–448×448 or foveal token count 1–5
encodings.y: CLIP cosine, DreamSim distance, or FID10K
encodings.facet: top blur sweep versus bottom token sweep
encodings.text: metric titles and ordered x labels

figures.data_and_statistics: A 2×3 grid reports three image-quality metrics under two one-factor ablations. Top panels vary ordered peripheral downsampling levels (28×28, 56×56, 112×112, 224×224, 448×448) with foveal tokens masked; bottom panels vary 1–5 randomly positioned foveal tokens with peripheral tokens masked. Axes are linear in the plotted numeric metric, x levels are categorical/ordered, and visible error bars lack a stated type or aggregation.
figures.evidence_relation: Appendix A.7 is the operating-point ablation behind the 0.25×/112×112 choice and the claim that peripheral conditioning carries more quality than sparse foveal-only input. It links image-generation quality to Figure 2 and the stream ablation in Figures 13–14; it is a sensitivity result, not behavioral evidence.
design_strengths: A fixed 2×3 arrangement keeps three complementary quality metrics aligned across two input ablations.
Ordered x labels expose the selected 112×112 point without hiding the full sweep.
Panel titles supply direct labels even without a formal legend.
design_weaknesses: Top and bottom rows have different independent variables, which can be missed when scanning columns.
Caption gives only directional findings and not the metric directions or uncertainty definition.
The identical single-series styling across panels makes panel-specific denominators and scale ranges easy to overlook.
figures.reusable_pattern: Align multiple quality metrics in a matrix, but place explicit row headers for the manipulated input stream and annotate the selected operating point rather than relying on prose alone.

figures.label: Figure 12

caption.text: Figure 12: Comparison of pixel-level (PSNR) and semantic (DreamSim) similarities in metameric judgments. (A, Left) portrays the histograms of PSNR values for generated images judged as “same” or “different” in the behavioral task, with nearly identical distributions between the two groups. (B, Right) shows the relationship between PSNR and DreamSim distances for all image pairs. There is a clear vertical separation by DreamSim distance that corresponds with metameric judgments, while PSNR values do not discriminate between what is considered metameric.

color.semantic_mapping: Green and orange distributions separate SAME and DIFFERENT outcomes in PSNR space; blue/purple point groups and pink callout boxes connect semantic distance to qualitative examples; gray grid and black text are neutral.

encodings.facet: A/B panels plus semantic/pixel callout examples

figures.data_and_statistics: Panel A is a density/histogram comparison of PSNR (dB) for same and different judgments; panel B is a PSNR-versus-DreamSim scatter with colored groups and horizontal/vertical separation guides. Pink callout examples label DIFF and SAME and annotate the opposing pixel-level/semantic-similarity directions. Both numeric axes are linear; distributions provide the uncertainty-like spread but no confidence interval or error bar.
figures.evidence_relation: Appendix A.8 tests whether pixel distance or semantic distance explains the behavioral decision. It supports the conclusion that DreamSim distance, rather than PSNR, separates same/different judgments and motivates the practical titration recommendation. The plot is a diagnostic of pair-level measurements, not a randomized treatment estimate.
design_strengths: The histogram, scatter, and concrete image callouts triangulate the same semantic-versus-pixel claim.
A legend plus direct SAME/DIFF labels makes the judgment mapping inspectable.
The separation guides make the qualitative decision boundary visually memorable without pretending PSNR is predictive.
design_weaknesses: The density normalization and number of image pairs are not stated in the figure.
The guide lines could be read as fitted decision thresholds although the caption describes separation rather than a classifier.
Multiple pastel hues and pink callout arrows are visually busy and not fully grayscale-safe.
figures.reusable_pattern: For competing similarity notions, combine marginal distributions, a joint scatter, and a few labeled exemplars; use direct labels and explicitly call guides descriptive rather than fitted thresholds.

figures.label: Figure 13

caption.text: Figure 13: Higher metameric (same) judgments for images incorporating both foveal and peripheral information. Using both foveal and peripheral features produced the highest fooling rates. Peripheral-only conditioning yielded the second best results, while foveal-only generations lagged significantly behind. Although the difference between peripheral-only and combined foveal-peripheral conditioning is small, it is meaningful: the additional high-resolution details from fixations lead participants to be more easily fooled.

color.semantic_mapping: Bar/card colors identify the input visual stream: combined foveal+peripheral (green/peach), peripheral-only (orange), and foveal-only (periwinkle/pink); black text and neutral image cells carry labels.

encodings.text: numeric rate labels and SAME/DIFF cards

figures.data_and_statistics: The top bar chart has four categorical conditions with labeled rates: Control 0.957, Both 0.545, Peripheral 0.458, and Foveal 0.084, on a linear 0–1 y axis. Arrows and colored cards below connect the three model ablations to original/generated SAME/DIFF examples. There is no uncertainty display, sample denominator, or formal legend; condition labels are direct.
figures.evidence_relation: Appendix A.9 is the central foveal/peripheral ablation evidence: it operationalizes §5.3’s 10-viewer task, places the 54.5/45.8/8.4% point estimates beside examples, and motivates the stream-specific feature replication in Figure 14. The control bar is a behavioral anchor, not a model stream.
design_strengths: Numeric bars and concrete examples share one decision surface, making the stream ablation easy to interpret.
Direct condition labels and arrows reduce dependence on a legend.
The large ordering gap between combined/peripheral and foveal-only is immediately visible.
design_weaknesses: Point rates lack uncertainty, viewer/trial denominator, and inferential comparison marks.
The four bars and three example cards do not make the control-vs-model relationship fully explicit.
Pastel colors encode streams but are not robust to grayscale or common color-vision deficiencies.
figures.reusable_pattern: Pair an ablation bar chart with one matched qualitative card per condition, and print exact rates on the bars so the visual examples cannot be mistaken for the estimate itself.

evidence.label: p.23 Figure 13 stream-ablation bars and example cards

figures.label: Figure 14

caption.text: Figure 14: Impact of input visual streams on hierarchical feature analyses. (Top Row) Multi-level feature analysis using neurally-grounded model (Jang & Tong, 2024) on driving metameric judgments. (Middle Row) Mid-level visual features driving metameric judgments (mid-level segmentation mIoU and SiLog depth estimation). (Bottom Row) High-level visual features driving metameric judgments (CLIP cosine similarity and DreamSim distance).

color.semantic_mapping: Green circles/solid lines represent combined foveal+peripheral, orange circles/solid lines peripheral-only, and blue circles/solid lines foveal-only; gray grids and black r,p annotations are neutral.

encodings.x: feature score (hierarchical cosine, depth, mIoU, CLIP, DreamSim)
encodings.text: shared legend and per-series r,p annotations

figures.data_and_statistics: Seven linear association panels are arranged in three processing-level rows: early/mid/late neural-layer cosine, SiLog depth and mIoU, then CLIP cosine and DreamSim distance. Three conditions—foveal+peripheral, peripheral-only, foveal-only—use green, orange, and blue circular lines with vertical error bars; a shared legend appears near the middle/right and each series has r,p annotations. The metric directions are heterogeneous and no uncertainty definition is supplied.
figures.evidence_relation: Appendix A.9 expands Figure 5 under the stream ablation and tests whether the same feature axes explain judgments equally across input conditions. It links Figure 13’s behavioral rates to the claim that full-model generations are more explainable, while identifying late-layer cosine and DreamSim as exceptions. This is the appendix’s strongest mechanism/heterogeneity object.
design_strengths: A shared x/y grammar makes cross-stream separation visible across seven feature axes.
The top/middle/bottom row structure mirrors the paper’s low-to-high processing narrative.
The legend and repeated r,p annotations expose both between-condition level shifts and within-condition associations.
design_weaknesses: Seven panels create high cognitive load and several panels use feature directions opposite to DreamSim/SiLog conventions.
A shared legend is distant from some panels, and small colored curves/annotations are difficult to read.
No formal uncertainty definition, sample size, or multiple-comparison context is visible.
figures.reusable_pattern: Replicate a main feature-analysis grammar for each ablation condition with a shared legend and row-level processing labels, but add explicit metric-direction and uncertainty keys when scaling beyond four panels.

figures.label: Figure 15

caption.text: Figure 15: FID and DreamSim evaluations based on DINOv2 and CLIP as vision encoders for foveal and peripheral feature extraction. (Left) The image generation quality (FID) for DINOv2-based peripheral generations is consistently better than CLIP patch embeddings. For DINOv2, we observe a sharp drop when decreasing the blur level, showing how decreasing blur results in the model encoding different, more accurate image features. This is not true for CLIP patch tokens, which seem to encode the same limited information across all blur levels. (Right) With increasing numbers of foveal token inputs, the DreamSim distance for both DINOv2 and CLIP-based embeddings decreases. However, DINOv2-based generations yield greater semantic similarities with the original images, especially at low token counts.

color.semantic_mapping: Orange and green curves distinguish CLIP ViT-L/14 and DINOv2-Base; gray grid and black labels are neutral; the legends repeat encoder identity within each panel.

encodings.x: ordered blur levels or foveal-token count
encodings.facet: blur sweep versus token sweep panels

figures.data_and_statistics: Two side-by-side linear plots compare DINOv2 and CLIP encoders. The left plots FID10K over ordered blur levels (28×28 through 448×448); the right plots DreamSim distance over 1–5 foveal tokens. Orange CLIP and green DINOv2 lines use circular markers, vertical error bars, light x/y grids, and separate legends. The x axes are ordered categorical levels rather than continuous distances.
figures.evidence_relation: Appendix A.10 directly validates the DINOv2 choice in Figure 1 by retraining a CLIP-conditioned model for a comparable ablation. It explains why DINOv2 preserves peripheral information and why low-token semantic similarity is better, connecting the encoder decision to Figure 16’s qualitative examples. Uncertainty and retraining seed details are absent.
design_strengths: The matched left/right ablations isolate peripheral blur sensitivity from foveal-token sensitivity.
A repeated two-color encoder legend makes the direct comparison easy to follow.
The caption states the direction of the FID and DreamSim findings rather than leaving the reader to infer metric orientation.
design_weaknesses: The x levels are categorical but visually connected as if continuous, which can imply interpolation between tested settings.
Error bars lack definitions and the 100K-versus-200K training difference is not encoded in the panels.
Orange/green curves remain color-dependent in grayscale.
figures.reusable_pattern: Use matched encoder curves over identical ablation levels, with per-panel legends and a caption that names the metric direction and training comparability boundary.

figures.label: Figure 16

caption.text: Figure 16: Image generation examples across blur levels using DINOv2 and CLIP as vision encoders. DINOv2-based peripheral generations resemble the original images more than CLIP-based generations, even at low blur levels. As the rate of downsampling decreases (28 × 28 → 448 × 448), DINOv2-based generations continue to show substantial improvements while CLIP-based generations exhibit minimal improvements. For the bottom two row pairs, DINOv2-based generations are able to keep the size of the plane (as well as its spatial position) intact irregardless of blur level input. However, that is not the case for the CLIP-based image generations.

color.semantic_mapping: Green/orange labels and row blocks identify DINOv2 versus CLIP; gray/white cells and black original/blur-level labels provide structural indexing.

encodings.facet: two scene examples × encoder rows × six columns

figures.data_and_statistics: A dense qualitative matrix shows two scene examples, each with DINOv2 and CLIP rows and columns for 28×28, 56×56, 112×112, 224×224, 448×448, and Original. Row labels directly name the encoders and column labels name blur levels. There are no axes, legend, numeric aggregation, or uncertainty marks; spatial arrangement is the primary encoding.
figures.evidence_relation: Appendix A.10 pairs the visual encoder curves in Figure 15 with concrete generations. The examples support the claim that DINOv2 retains plane size/position and improves as blur is reduced, whereas CLIP changes little; they are qualitative evidence for encoder selection, not a representative sample estimate.
design_strengths: The fixed blur-level columns make the DINOv2/CLIP comparison visually direct.
Including the Original column establishes a reference endpoint for every row.
Row/column labels make this dense montage navigable without a color legend.
design_weaknesses: Only two scene examples are shown and selection is not described.
Image cells are small and visual quality judgments are subjective without a paired metric annotation.
“Irregardless” in the caption is imprecise prose, and the figure cannot expose whether apparent improvements generalize beyond the examples.
figures.reusable_pattern: For encoder ablations, place matched rows over an ordered degradation axis and include the original endpoint; keep the montage explicitly qualitative and let the adjacent curves carry population-level evidence.

cross_object_system.visual_narrative: Figure 1 defines the foveal/peripheral conditioning interface; Figure 2 selects an image-quality operating point; Figure 3 makes same/different judgments concrete; Figures 4–5 connect those judgments to neural, mid-level, and semantic feature axes. Appendix Figure 6 specifies the real-time task, Figures 7–8 extend the mechanism to low-level texture and object localization, Figures 9–10 add qualitative condition-specific examples, Figures 11–12 test quality/similarity diagnostics, Figures 13–14 isolate stream contributions, and Figures 15–16 validate the DINOv2 encoder choice. The sequence is mechanism → qualitative outcome → correlational mechanism → ablation/diagnostic boundary.
cross_object_system.caption_system: All 16 captions begin with a Figure label and object title. Main Figures 1, 3–5 and most appendix figures use a bold or medium-looking title phrase followed by setup, encoding/key, comparison, and directional finding; Figures 2, 9, 10, and 14 are more descriptive and leave key sampling/uncertainty details to surrounding prose. Captions frequently define salmon/turquoise or metric direction, but no caption defines the error-bar type, denominator, seed, or aggregation unit.
cross_object_system.table_header_system: No Table object appears in the 26-page PDF, including the appendix; therefore there is no observed table header, row-group, rule, precision, or highlighting system to audit. Numeric evidence is carried by plots and prose instead.
cross_object_system.method_result_ablation_link: The dual-stream architecture in Figure 1 is tested through image-quality tuning (Figure 2), behavioral same/different evidence (Figure 3), feature associations (Figures 4–5), and stream/encoder/blur/token ablations (Figures 11, 13–16). Figures 7–8 add independent feature probes rather than changing the model. The visual system generally preserves the distinction between model input manipulation, feature measurement, and participant judgment.
cross_object_system.main_appendix_link: The main text contains Figures 1–5; Appendix A.1 Figure 6 supplies timing and online API details, A.5 Figures 7–8 expand low-level/object analyses, A.6 Figures 9–10 extend qualitative examples, A.7 Figure 11 varies blur/tokens, A.8 Figure 12 contrasts PSNR/DreamSim, A.9 Figures 13–14 ablate streams, and A.10 Figures 15–16 compare DINOv2 with CLIP. The main captions point to A.6 and the body points to the remaining appendix modules, but several crucial denominators and uncertainty definitions remain prose-only.
cross_object_system.typography_consistency: PDF captions and body text consistently use embedded Nimbus Roman No9 L regular/medium/italic with Computer Modern math. Figure interiors use raster sans-serif labels with estimated 5–11 pt text; architecture/timeline headers are larger. The caption/body type is stable, but plot label sizes and raster sharpness vary markedly across objects.
cross_object_system.color_consistency: Salmon own-fixation versus turquoise/green random-fixation curves recur in Figures 4, 5, 7, and 8, while stream ablations use green/orange/blue/pink in Figures 13–16. Green/red bordered qualitative blocks consistently mean SAME/DIFFERENT. Marker and line style often duplicate quantitative hue, but bars, montages, and some encoder comparisons rely mainly on color and are not consistently grayscale-safe.

most_reusable_patterns: Use a single two-branch architecture diagram with identical downstream endpoint to expose foveal/peripheral mechanism and its method-interface boundary.
Keep own/random conditions visually stable with hue plus marker/line-style redundancy across feature-analysis panels.
Pair quantitative ablation bars or curves with matched qualitative image cards, and print exact rates or ordered levels directly in the object.
Use a fixed qualitative SAME/DIFFERENT grid across human-fixation and random-fixation conditions so only the manipulated input changes.
For competing similarity measures, combine marginal distributions, a joint scatter, and a few labeled exemplars rather than relying on one metric plot.
highest_value_objects: Figure 1: clearest method-interface and training/inference conditioning map.
Figure 4: strongest visual bridge from neural hierarchy proxies to same-judgment outcome.
Figure 13: compact stream ablation with exact fooling rates plus qualitative checks.
Figure 14: broadest stream-specific mechanism replication across seven feature axes.
Figure 12: most persuasive triangulation of semantic versus pixel similarity.
failure_patterns: All quantitative figures omit a clear definition of error bars, sample denominator, aggregation unit, and random seed.
Many raster composites use small labels and hue-dependent encodings, weakening grayscale and low-resolution readability.
Qualitative montages show representative examples without selection rules or IDs, so they cannot substitute for population-level estimates.
Heterogeneous metric directions (SiLog/DreamSim versus mIoU/CLIP) and categorical ablation levels are visually connected without a complete direction/scale key.
The PDF contains no Table object and therefore lacks a compact, auditable tabular summary of participant counts, rates, and uncertainty.
final_judgment.one_sentence_visual_strategy: The paper visualizes a dual-stream foveal/peripheral generator, makes its behavioral judgments concrete with matched image grids, then layers correlated feature panels and appendix ablations to argue that semantic and structured scene information—not pixel distance alone—supports metameric perception.
